intro.en: Age 22. You got a job as an accounts assistant in town: ₹15,000 a month. Ammamma frames your first payslip. Nanna still works the cotton field, coughing more than he admits.

objective.en: Your first salary just arrived! Go to the office.

text.en: Your first salary hits the account. Colleagues want a party at the dhaba: ₹3,000. Amma needs ₹2,000 for Chinni's nursing coaching. And a shiny phone is on 'no-cost EMI'.

label.en: Pay yourself first: ₹3,000 into an emergency fund, then Chinni's ₹2,000

outcome.en: You set up an auto-transfer on salary day. The money you never see is the money you never miss.

why.en: 'Pay yourself first' means saving the moment money arrives, not whatever is left at month-end.

label.en: Party tonight! And the new phone on EMI

outcome.en: Best night of the year. The phone's 'no-cost' EMI has a ₹900 processing fee and a ₹199 'protection plan' you never asked for.

why.en: 'No-cost' EMIs hide fees. And EMIs taken in the first month quietly eat every future salary.

label.en: Send ₹8,000 home and keep a little

outcome.en: Amma cries on the phone. Nanna pretends he isn't. Your own pocket is nearly empty again.

why.en: Helping family is good. Without your own emergency fund, the next shock hits all of you.

objective.en: Policy Ramana is at your home. It's lunchtime, of course.

text.en: {cast:agent} finishes his second plate and opens a glossy file: "Endowment plan! ₹30,000 a year, money back after 20 years!" Your office offers family [[insurance]] instead: ₹6,000 a year for ₹3 lakh cover.

label.en: Take the office family health cover, a cheap [[term_insurance]], and enrol Nanna's crop in [[pmfby]]

outcome.en: Three policies for about ₹7,500 a year. Ramana leaves without dessert.

why.en: Insurance is for disasters you can't afford, not for investing. Keep insurance and investing separate.

label.en: Sign Ramana's endowment plan

outcome.en: The 'returns' work out to about 4% a year, and the life cover is tiny. Ramana's commission: ₹9,000.

why.en: Mixed insurance-plus-savings plans pay big commissions and give small cover and small returns.

label.en: Skip it. Nothing will happen to us

outcome.en: Ramana sighs and eats a banana for the road. You save ₹6,000 a year. For now.

why.en: One hospital bill can wipe out years of savings. Health cover is cheapest when you're young and healthy.

objective.en: Nanna collapsed in the cotton field! Rush to the hospital!

note.en: You arrived late. Amma had to sign the papers alone.

text.en: Nanna had a heart attack. The hospital needs ₹1,80,000 for surgery by tomorrow morning. Amma holds his hand. Everyone looks at you.

label.en: Use the family health insurance

outcome.en: The insurance desk approves it in four hours. You pay ₹0. Nanna wakes up and asks for tea.

why.en: This is exactly what insurance is for: a big bill you could never pay alone.

label.en: Use your savings, and a bank personal loan for the rest

outcome.en: Kavitha akka rushes the loan through by evening: 13% a year. Nanna is saved. The EMI will be with you for three years.

why.en: When you must borrow, a bank loan at 13% costs far less than a loan app or the sahukar. An [[emergency_fund]] would have cost nothing.

label.en: Instant loan app: ₹1,50,000 in five minutes

warn.en: [[loan_app]]s charge 36% a year or more, plus 10% fees, and illegal ones steal your contacts and harass your family. A bank loan is less than half the cost.

outcome.en: The money arrives in four minutes, minus a ₹15,000 'processing fee'. The app asked for your contacts. You clicked 'Allow'.

why.en: Fast and easy is how loan apps hook you. The real cost appears later.

label.en: Narsaiah sahukar. He never says no

outcome.en: Narsaiah hands over the cash and takes Nanna's land papers 'just for safekeeping'.

why.en: 24% a year, and your family's land as security. Expensive debt in an emergency is how families lose land.

objective.en: Your phone won't stop buzzing. Open it (press P).

text.en: You missed one payment by a day. Now the app is sending YOUR photo, edited as a 'FRAUD' poster, to everyone in your contacts. Ammamma got it too.

label.en: Take a second app loan to pay the first

warn.en: Paying a loan with another loan is a spiral: each new app adds fees and interest. In months you'll owe triple. Stop here and ask for help.

outcome.en: It works for 11 days. Then both apps call. Then a third app offers 'help'.

why.en: New debt to pay old debt only delays the crash and makes it bigger.

label.en: Report the app to the police and RBI's Sachet portal, then go to the bank

outcome.en: The app isn't RBI-registered. The police block its harassment numbers. You still owe the money, but only the fair amount.

why.en: Illegal loan apps can be reported. Harassment is a crime. Check any lender on RBI's list first.

label.en: Sit your family down and tell them everything

outcome.en: Amma is angry for ten minutes. Then she takes out her savings-group book: "We'll fix this together."

why.en: Debt grows in secret. Telling people who care about you opens cheaper ways out.

objective.en: Recovery agents are shouting outside your home. Go home, now.

text.en: Seven apps. ₹3,10,000 owed. Two recovery agents are shouting at Amma in the street, and the neighbours are watching. Chinni is hiding inside.

label.en: Sell Amma's gold, borrow from the savings group, and close every app

outcome.en: Amma's wedding bangles go to the bank's gold counter. The apps go silent. Nobody talks at dinner for a week.

why.en: Closing the costliest debt first, even painfully, is how a spiral stops.

label.en: Switch off your phone and leave for Hyderabad

warn.en: Running doesn't stop the interest, the harassment of your family, or the damage to your [[credit_score]]. Every month away makes it worse.

outcome.en: You sleep on a friend's floor in Hyderabad. The agents keep visiting Amma instead.

why.en: Debt doesn't disappear when you do. Lenders go after the family and the credit record follows you.

objective.en: Go to the bank. Kavitha akka can help you get out of this.

text.en: {cast:banker} lists your loans on paper, costliest first. "Loan app 36%, then the rest. We close the most expensive one first. Always."

label.en: Take one bank loan at 13% to close the loan app today

outcome.en: One loan, one EMI, one fair rate. The app's number is blocked. You sleep through the night for the first time in months.

why.en: Swapping a 36% loan for a 13% loan cuts the cost by more than half. Always repay the highest rate first.

label.en: Prepay the app from every salary until it's gone

outcome.en: Dal and rice for six months. The app balance falls, slowly.

why.en: Prepaying costly debt is the best 'investment' you can make: it 'earns' you the interest rate you stop paying.

objective.en: Chintu is back in the village in a white shirt and a gold watch. He's at the square.

text.en: Chintu now works for {cast:tempter}'s new company: Golden Harvest Gold Scheme. "Pay ₹1 lakh, get ₹5,000 every month, forever! Half the village joined!" He shows a stamped certificate.

label.en: Invest ₹50,000. Half the village can't be wrong

warn.en: ₹5,000 a month on ₹1 lakh is 60% a year. Schemes that pay old members with new members' money are [[ponzi]] schemes. They always collapse.

outcome.en: The first ₹2,500 arrives on time. And the second. You tell two colleagues about it.

why.en: Ponzi schemes pay early on purpose, so investors bring in more people. It ends when new money stops.

label.en: Ask to see its registration with SEBI or the Registrar of Chits

outcome.en: The 'certificate' is from a Dubai company and spells 'Goverment' wrong. You take a photo. Chintu looks uncomfortable.

why.en: Legal schemes are registered and can show it. A stamp and a smile are not registration.

label.en: Refuse politely

outcome.en: "Your loss, boss," says Chintu, sounding exactly like Prakash.

why.en: Saying no to 'guaranteed' returns is always safe.

text.en: Nanna's heart attack cost you a week of worry and ₹0. Ramana now tells other families: "That one? Can't sell them anything."
Nanna is home, and you are paying off the hospital bill one EMI at a time. Not a disaster. But you now know the price of having no [[emergency_fund]].
Every month ₹2,500 arrives from Golden Harvest, like clockwork. You start to believe. You don't notice that it's just your own money coming back.
The loan apps are silent, Amma's gold is gone, and you have a long list of EMIs. You got out. Many people don't.
₹3 lakh owed to seven apps, a family harassed, and a credit record in ruins. No bank will lend to you for seven years. It started with one 'instant' loan.
